classes.name: AsyncConnectionWrapper
classes.docu:
This wraps an AsyncConnection but only allows _using_ the AsyncConnection,
not manipulation (closing, etc.).

methods.name: sendRequest
methods.docu:
This method should never take very long although it might block waiting
for the transport (socket, for example). It will never block waiting for
an actual response to a request. The user is not allowed to send a
request without a response handler to avoid letting the response queue
grow without bound. This will throw an exception if either there are no
AsyncSinks in this connection or there is a serialization problem.

**Returns:** T extends AsyncRequestV,E>, V>

for the transport (socket, for example). It pushes a request to the other

there is a serialization problem.

methods.name: sendRequest
methods.docu:
This method should never take very long although it might block waiting
for the transport (socket, for example). It will never block waiting for
an actual response to a request. The user is not allowed to send a
request without a response handler to avoid letting the response queue
grow without bound. This will throw an exception if either there are no
AsyncSinks in this connection or there is a serialization problem. The
"sync" parameters request that the request and/or response be processed
by the socket thread instead of a worker thread. This marginally speeds
up the processing (on my machine ~1/10000 ms) at the expense of blocking
other requests/responses from using the socket. Usually you do not want
to do this, but if the processing time is short or you don't care about
other traffic then you can request it.

**Parameters:**

- `p_syncRequest`
- `p_syncResponse`

**Returns:** T extends AsyncRequestV,E>, V>

classes.name: AsyncExecutor
classes.docu:
This is just a tag interface for individual implementation Executor
interfaces that will actually implement the visitor part of the visitor
pattern. This does not actually specify an execute method because no generic
execute method makes sense.

classes.name: AsyncResponseHandler
classes.docu: Actually handle one or more responses to an AsyncRequest.

methods.name: processResponse
methods.docu:
This method will be called in its' own thread and is therefore allowed to
take as long as necessary. Be aware that if the same handler is
registered for several requests it can be called simultaneously from
different threads and should be smart enough to handle it. The other
arguments allow for an entire list of responses to a single request to be
processed, possibly out of order. The index is zero based.

**Parameters:**

- `p_response`

methods.name: processThrowableResponse
methods.docu:
This method will be called if a throwable is thrown during processing. It
is always the last response that will be received and will therefore
signals the end of responses.

**Parameters:**

- `p_throwable`

classes.name: AsyncConnection
classes.docu:
Main connection interface. This connection will internally have a AsyncSink
for handling the actual connection as well as an AsyncSinkQueue and
AsyncSourceQueue for handling the request and response processing.

requests and responses. An AsyncRequestIdFactory must be provided to
create the appropriate AsyncRequestIds. A AsyncRequestIdMemorys should be

- `p_version`
- `p_sink`
- `p_idFactory`
- `p_localMemory`
- `p_remoteMemory`
- `p_asyncExecutor`

classes.name: AsyncSink

Interface that actually pushes requests and responses to the other side of a
connection. All methods of this class are allowed to block on the connection,
but should not do any actual work beyond what is necessary to send the
request or response.

methods.docu:

serialization problem.

methods.name: sendResponse
methods.docu:
This method takes a response and hands it off to the other side of the

serialization problem.

classes.name: AsyncRequestIdMemory
classes.docu:
Allow dependencies to be implemented by allowing a connection to check to see
whether an AsyncRequestId has been processed. If this is not implemented then
dependencies will error. Clearly the design of the AsyncRequestId must take
this into account. It would be a huge mistake to just keep a Set of processed
AsyncRequestIds lying around since over the lifetime of a connection there
could be millions or more requests. Therefore your best bet would ideally be
able to collapse an entire range or AsyncRequestIds. Alternatively you could
implement a memory timeout where old AsyncRequestIds are forgotten after some
period. Another option would be to only remember a limited number of
AsyncRequestIds and push them out of memory using FIFO.

classes.name: StreamSerializable
classes.docu:
Generic interface for classes that we want to be able to write to a stream in
such a way that it can easily be extracted by a language other than Java.
This, of course, means that it cannot use Java serialization. This allows the
object to substitute some other generic mechanism. Implementing classes
should all have a default constructor, just like Serializable.

**Parameters:**

- `p_out`

classes.name: AsyncRequestId
classes.docu:
The request id is determined strictly by the side of the connection sending
the request. It will be used as a key in a Map (for responses), so it needs
to be immutable and have 'hashCode' and 'equals' implemented correctly.
